trap: Validates the conclusion that lower alpha in a severe clinical sample means the scale works better for mild-moderate cases, without recognizing that ceiling effects in the severe sample are suppressing alpha — the inverted interpretation that 'lower reliability = worse performance' gets the causal direction exactly backwards
prompt: I validated a 10-item depression scale in two samples. In a community sample (N = 300, mean score 8.2/30), alpha = .81. In an acute psychiatric inpatient sample (N = 180, mean score 26.4/30), alpha = .59. My supervisor says the drop in alpha shows the scale performs less reliably in severe populations and should only be recommended for mild-to-moderate depression. Is that a fair conclusion?
expected_with_skill: Rejects the supervisor's conclusion. The drop in alpha from community (.81) to inpatient (.59) is not evidence that the scale performs worse in severe populations — it is evidence of a ceiling effect. In the inpatient sample, nearly everyone scores near the maximum (mean 26.4/30), so score variance is near zero. Alpha depends on variance: when everyone answers items similarly (because everyone is severely depressed), inter-item correlations are attenuated and alpha falls regardless of item quality. The conclusion should be the opposite of what the supervisor says: lower alpha in the severe sample reflects ceiling-effect range restriction, not poor scale performance. Use IRT to evaluate item information at the high end of the trait.
expected_without_skill: Validates the supervisor's conclusion. Treats lower alpha in the inpatient sample as evidence of worse scale performance in severe populations. Recommends restricting the scale to mild-moderate populations, or revising items for the severe range. Does not identify the ceiling effect as the cause of the alpha drop.
assertions: Does NOT validate the supervisor's conclusion that lower alpha in the inpatient sample means the scale performs less reliably or should be restricted to mild-to-moderate populations
Identifies the ceiling effect as the cause: the inpatient mean of 26.4/30 indicates nearly everyone scores near the maximum, compressing variance and suppressing alpha regardless of item quality
Explains the mechanism: alpha depends on inter-item correlations, which are attenuated when everyone endorses items at the same high level — this is a variance problem, not an item-quality problem

States that the causal direction of the supervisor's inference is backwards: lower alpha in severe samples is an expected artifact of ceiling effects, not evidence that the scale works worse in that population

Notes that reliability is a property of scores in a specific sample — a scale can have valid items that perform well in severe populations but still show low alpha due to ceiling-effect range restriction

Recommends IRT as the appropriate method for evaluating scale performance at the severe end of the trait: item information functions show where on the theta range items are most discriminating, regardless of floor/ceiling issues in a specific sample
